newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy says elections the key to Albania's future.
newsitem.headline: Italy says elections the key to Albania's future.

text.p: Italy told Albania's squabbling political parties on Monday that international aid for economic recovery in their violence-plagued country would not be possible without free and fair elections.

Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini sounded the warning in an opening speech to an international meeting in Rome on the crisis in Albania, Europe's poorest country, where early elections are scheduled for June 29.
Preparations for the vote have been dogged by disputes over how they will be conducted and supervised.

"Without the consolidation of the national reconciliation process, without elections, conducted in a safe and fair environment accroding to international standards, without rules of conduct shared and agreed by all parties in Albania, the conditions for recovery in the economic and financial fields will not be present," Dini said in his speech.
"Therefore I urge Albania in a spirit of friendship to speed up the reconciliation process and to fully cooperate with the OSCE, especially in view of the forthcoming elections," he said.

The meeting in Rome was being attended by Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, European mediator Franz Vranitzky of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and senior diplomats from the European Union and the United States.

Major international organisations, including the World Bank and International Monetary Fund were also present at the day-long talks, intended to prepare the way for a full ministerial conference on Albania, tentatively set for mid-June.
Dini said the conference agenda should focus on political as well as economic and financial issues.

Albania vitally needs the election to restore law and order after anger over the collapse of get-rich-quick pyramid investment schemes erupted in February and March into rebellion against President Sali Berisha.
Although the situation has calmed since the arrival in April of an Italian-led multinational security force, large swathes of the country remain outside government control.
More than a million weapons looted during the troubles have fallen into private hands.
Fino, of the opposition Socialists, heads a nine-party interim national unity government installed in March to lead the Balkan country up until the elections.
Berisha has been at odds with the government over several issues and on Sunday rejected a cabinet call to lift a curfew before next month's elections.

The curfew was established under a state of emergency imposed in March by the outgoing parliament, which was dominated by Berisha's Democratic Party. Berisha dissolved the assembly in early May in preparation for the elections.
